reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard metabolic references
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by deficiency of the enzyme galactocerebrosidase (galactosylceramidase), leading to demyelination and formation of characteristic multinucleated globoid cells
The classic early-infantile form presents in the first months with irritability, feeding difficulty, stiffness, and hyperirritability, followed by rapid neurodegeneration
Marked irritability, hypertonicity, and exaggerated startle to stimuli are prominent early features
Accumulation of the toxic metabolite psychosine (galactosylsphingosine) is central to the destruction of myelin-forming cells
Peripheral neuropathy with slowed nerve conduction and raised cerebrospinal fluid protein commonly accompany the central disease
Later-onset (late-infantile, juvenile, and adult) forms present with more insidious motor, visual, and cognitive decline
MRI shows white matter change, and globoid cells are a defining pathological hallmark
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in presymptomatic infants can alter the course, while symptomatic infantile disease responds poorly
reference.pathophysiology: Krabbe disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in GALC, encoding the lysosomal enzyme galactocerebrosidase. Deficient activity impairs degradation of galactolipids found in myelin, notably galactosylceramide, and leads to accumulation of the cytotoxic metabolite psychosine (galactosylsphingosine). Psychosine is toxic to oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, causing widespread loss of myelin-forming cells and demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous system. The pathological response includes infiltration by characteristic multinucleated macrophages (globoid cells), giving the alternative name globoid cell leukodystrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Non-accidental injury or other causes of infantile irritability and hypertonia
additionalInvestigations: Assay of galactocerebrosidase enzyme activity, including newborn screening in some programmes
GALC molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Psychosine measurement to support diagnosis and assess severity
Brain MRI to characterise white matter involvement
Nerve conduction studies and cerebrospinal fluid protein assessment
redFlags: Extreme irritability with hypertonia and feeding failure in early infancy
Emerging seizures or loss of vision
reference.prognosis: The early-infantile form is rapidly progressive and usually fatal within the first few years of life. Later-onset forms progress more slowly and variably. Stem cell transplantation offers benefit mainly when performed in presymptomatic infants, and once symptoms are established the outlook remains poor.
pitfalls: Mistaking early extreme irritability and stiffness for colic, reflux, or a behavioural problem
Confusing it with metachromatic leukodystrophy without appropriate enzyme testing
Missing the narrow presymptomatic window for transplantation
Overlooking peripheral neuropathy as a supportive diagnostic clue
management: Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only disease-modifying option, of benefit mainly in presymptomatic infants identified on newborn screening or in early later-onset disease
Antispasticity agents such as baclofen and measures to control the marked irritability
Nutritional support and feeding management, including gastrostomy, for feeding difficulty
Respiratory care with secretion management and physiotherapy for tone and contractures
Occupational therapy and communication aids for slower later-onset forms
Genetic counselling and family testing, reflecting autosomal recessive GALC inheritance
Multidisciplinary palliative and supportive care given the progressive, often fatal course
